claim: Multiple BMP-dependent Smad-binding elements (SBEs) are present in the 1.1 kb 5' upstream region of both human PPIF and mouse Ppif genes.
source: We found multiple BMP-dependent Smad-binding elements (SBEs) in the 1.1 kb 5' upstream region of both human PPIF and mouse Ppif genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on in silico analysis using PROMO online platform and shown in Figure 1A diagram.

claim: Smad1 overexpression downregulates CypD mRNA expression in ST2 and MC3T3-e1 cells.
source: We observed that CypD mRNA was downregulated after Smad1 overexpression, whereas osteogenic marker Runx2, a readout of BMP/Smad activity, was upregulated (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: Real-time RT-qPCR data from transfection experiments shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: BMP2 treatment significantly induces Smad1-Ppif promoter interaction.
source: Importantly, BMP2 treatment significantly induced Smad1-Ppif interaction. Band density quantification revealed 2.5-fold increase of Smad1-Ppif interaction in the BMP2-treated samples (Figure 2C).
evidence: ChIP assay data with PCR analysis and band density quantification shown in Figure 2.

claim: Smad1 binds the CypD gene (Ppif) promoter in BMP-dependent manner.
source: These results demonstrate that Smad1 binds the CypD gene (Ppif) promoter in BMP-dependent manner.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ChIP assay results showing increased Smad1-Ppif interaction with BMP2 treatment.

claim: Smad1 significantly decreases the luciferase signal from the 1.1 kb Ppif-luc promoter-reporter.
source: Figure 3C shows that Smad1 significantly decreased the luciferase signal from the 1.1 kb Ppif-luc promoter-reporter.
evidence: Dual luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only the full-length 1.1 kb Ppif-luc reporter showed Ppif activity repression upon Smad1 transfection.
source: Thus, only the full-length 1.1 kb Ppif-luc reporter showed Ppif activity repression upon Smad1 transfection (Figure 3C).
evidence: Comparison of luciferase reporter assays with different promoter constructs shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMP/Smad signaling is a transcriptional repressor of CypD.
source: In sum, our data indicate that BMP/Smad signaling is a transcriptional repressor of CypD.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches including transfection, ChIP, and luciferase reporter assays.

claim: Inhibitory Smad7 rescues Ppif promoter activity in Smad1-transfected cells.
source: To further delineate the role of BMP/Smad signaling in Ppif repression, we used the inhibitory Smad7 which rescued Ppif promoter activity in Smad1-transfected cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data with Smad7 co-transfection shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 1.1 kb mutated Ppif-luc reporter co-transfected with pCMV-Smad1 rescued Ppif promoter activity.
source: The 1.1 kb mutated Ppif-luc reporter co-transfected with pCMV-Smad1 rescued Ppif promoter activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay with SBE-mutated promoter construct shown in Figure 3D.

claim: BMP2 and osteogenic media downregulate the luciferase signal from the Ppif promoter reporter, whereas Noggin rescues Ppif activity.
source: BMP2 and osteogenic media downregulated the luciferase signal, whereas Noggin rescued Ppif activity (Figure 3E).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data with BMP2 treatment and Noggin inhibition shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mouse myogenic C2C12 cell line showed opposite effects on Ppif promoter activity under BMP-dependent Smad activation compared to osteogenic cells.
source: However, the mouse myogenic C2C12 cell line showed opposite effects under BMP-dependent Smad activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data in C2C12 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PPIF activity is regulated by Smad-dependent signaling in myogenic cells but the direction of PPIF regulation is tissue specific.
source: These findings show that PPIF activity is also regulated by Smad-dependent signaling in myogenic cells but suggest that the direction of PPIF regulation is tissue specific.
evidence: Inference from comparison of osteogenic and myogenic cell responses to Smad1 activation.

claim: BMP/Smad signaling transcriptionally represses Ppif promoter activity in osteogenic cells regardless of their embryonic origin.
source: Taken together, these data support our hypothesis that BMP/Smad signaling transcriptionally represses Ppif promoter activity in osteogenic cells regardless of their embryonic origin and consequently downregulates CypD expression during osteogenic differentiation.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experiments in both mesodermal (ST2) and neural crest-derived (MC3T3-e1) osteogenic cells.

claim: Primary BMSCs, ST2 cells, and MC3T3-e1 cells undergo osteoblast differentiation confirmed by alkaline phosphate and alizarin red staining.
source: Figure 4 shows that primary BMSCs isolated from mouse long bones, mouse bone marrow-derived osteogenic cell line ST2, and mouse calvaria-derived osteogenic cell line MC3T3-e1 underwent OB differentiation confirmed by alkaline phosphate and alizarin red staining (Figure 4A–B)
evidence: Histological staining data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Osteogenic differentiation is accompanied by upregulation of osteogenic markers Alp and Bglap in BMSCs, ST2, and MC3T3-e1 cells.
source: Figure 4 shows that primary BMSCs isolated from mouse long bones, mouse bone marrow-derived osteogenic cell line ST2, and mouse calvaria-derived osteogenic cell line MC3T3-e1 underwent OB differentiation confirmed by alkaline phosphate and alizarin red staining (Figure 4A–B) and upregulation of osteogenic markers Alp and Bglap.(Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Osteogenic differentiation is accompanied by downregulation of CypD gene (Ppif) mRNA expression in BMSCs, ST2, and MC3T3-e1 cells.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, osteogenic differentiation was accompanied by downregulation of CypD gene, Ppif, mRNA expression in all these cell types (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Human BMSCs show downregulation of CypD gene (PPIF) mRNA expression during osteogenic differentiation.
source: To confirm that this effect is not species-specific, we analyzed human BMSC RNAseq dataset from our previous publication (Shum et al., 2016a) and observed downregulation of CypD gene, PPIF, mRNA expression in osteoinduced cells when compared to undifferentiated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNAseq data analysis from previous publication shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CypD protein content decreases during osteoblast differentiation.
source: Protein content of CypD correspondingly decreased during OB differentiation as measured with western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MPTP activity decreases during osteoblast differentiation as measured by calcein-cobalt assay.
source: The assay showed that calcein signal increased at day 14 of OB differentiation when compared to day 0 indicating lower MPTP activity (Figure 4F).
evidence: Calcein-cobalt assay data measured by flow cytometry shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mitochondrial mass does not change during osteoblast differentiation.
source: No changes were detected in the total mitochondrial mass during OB differentiation as labeled by nonyl acridine orange (Figure 4G), therefore confirming that calcein signal increase is in fact caused by a lower pore activity and not by an increased mitochondrial compartment.
evidence: NAO staining data measured by flow cytometry shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CypD expression is downregulated and MPTP activity is decreased during osteogenic differentiation.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that CypD expression is downregulated and MPTP activity is decreased during osteogenic differentiation.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on mRNA, protein, and functional MPTP assay data.

claim: Wnt3a at concentrations of 25 ng and above showed no effect on Ppif promoter activity.
source: Even Wnt3a concentrations of 25 ng and above, previously reported to activate OB differentiation and mitochondrial function in osteogenic cells (Smith and Eliseev, 2021), showed no effect on Ppif activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Dose-response luciferase reporter assay data with Wnt3a treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 143b osteosarcoma cells cannot undergo osteogenic differentiation due to Runx2 proteasomal degradation.
source: We previously reported that the human osteosarcoma (OS) cell line 143b cannot undergo osteogenic differentiation due to Runx2 proteasomal degradation (Shapovalov et al., 2010).
evidence: Reference to previous publication by the authors.

claim: 143b osteosarcoma cells fail to upregulate late osteogenic markers (IBSP, BGLAP) upon BMP2 treatment despite upregulating early marker RUNX2.
source: We confirmed the 143b-OS cells' inability to fully differentiate upon BMP2 osteogenic induction by comparing their mRNA expression of osteoblastic differentiation markers to that of human non-cancerous osteoblastic cell line, hFOB (Figure 5A). While hFOB cells upregulate ALP, IBSP, and BGLAP, 143b cells fail to upregulate these osteogenic markers.
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR data comparing hFOB and 143b cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Smad1 transfection leads to downregulation of CypD mRNA expression in 143b osteosarcoma cells.
source: As seen in the ST2 and MC3T3e1 cell lines, pCMV-Smad1 transfection led to downregulation of CypD mRNA expression in 143b-OS cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR data from 143b cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Smad1 decreases Ppif promoter activity when co-transfected with the full-length 1.1 kb Ppif-luc reporter in 143b osteosarcoma cells.
source: As seen in the ST2 and MC3T3e1 cell lines, pCMV-Smad1 transfection led to downregulation of CypD mRNA expression in 143b-OS cells (Figure 5B) and decreased Ppif promoter activity when co-transfected with the full-length 1.1 kb Ppif-luc reporter (Figure 5C).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data from 143b cells shown in Figure 5C.

claim: BMP/Smad signaling exerts inhibitory effect on the Ppif gene as a direct transcriptional repressor and not as an indirect result of osteogenic differentiation.
source: Altogether, our data strongly indicate that BMP/Smad signaling exerts inhibitory effect on the Ppif gene as a direct transcriptional repressor and not as an indirect result of osteogenic differentiation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Conclusion based on experiments in differentiation-arrested 143b cells showing Ppif repression by Smad1.

claim: CypD knock-out mice present with higher BMSC OxPhos function and osteogenic potential.
source: We previously reported that CypD knock-out (KO) mice, a loss-of-function (LOF) model of the MPTP, present with higher BMSC OxPhos function and osteogenic potential (Shum et al., 2016b).
evidence: Reference to previous publication by the authors.

claim: CypD KO BMSCs present pro-osteogenic gene signatures based on RNAseq transcriptome analysis.
source: Moreover, RNAseq transcriptome analysis showed that CypD KO BMSCs present pro-osteogenic gene signatures (Shares et al., 2020).
evidence: Reference to previous publication by the authors.

claim: MC3T3e1 cells expressing constitutively active CypD (caCypD) K166Q mutant show impaired osteogenic differentiation.
source: Cells expressing caCypD showed impaired osteogenic differentiation as evidenced by lower expression of OB marker genes, Runx2, Alp, and Bglap, at both days 7 and 14 in osteogenic media (Figure 6B).
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR data from caCypD-expressing MC3T3e1 cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Osteoblast-specific, inducible 2.3 kb Col1CreERt2;R26caPpif/+ BMSCs are incapable of completing osteoblast differentiation.
source: Osteoinduced caCypD-expressing cells presented with decreased osteogenic differentiation and OB markers when compared to control cells (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Histological staining and RT-PCR data from BMSCs of Col1CreERt2;R26caPpif/+ mice shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: CypD overexpression decreases TMRE signal and mitochondrial function in BMSCs and osteoblasts.
source: CypD overexpression clearly decreased TMRE signal, and therefore mitochondrial function and OxPhos capacity in infected, eGFP-expressing Cre+, cells compared to non-infected, Cre-, cells in both BMSCs at day 0 and OBs at day 11 (Figure 6H and J).
evidence: TMRE fluorescence microscopy data from adeno-Cre infected R26caPpif/+ BMSCs shown in Figure 6H and J.

claim: Downregulation of CypD is an important part of osteogenic program.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that CypD GOF disrupts mitochondrial function and impairs OB differentiation and thus, downregulation of CypD is an important part of osteogenic program.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on gain-of-function experiments in vitro and in vivo.

claim: Downregulation of BMP/Smad signaling markers is accompanied by significant upregulation of CypD gene (Ppif) in aged mouse bones.
source: In particular, downregulation of markers of BMP/Smad signaling was accompanied by significant upregulation of CypD gene, Ppif, in aged mouse bones (top left table).
evidence: Analysis of publicly available RNAseq dataset on bone aging shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upregulation of BMP/Smad signaling during active phase of bone formation (day 14 post-fracture) in mouse fracture callus is accompanied by significant downregulation of Ppif.
source: On the other hand, upregulation of BMP/Smad signaling during active phase of bone formation (day 14 post-fracture) in mouse fracture callus was accompanied by significant downregulation of Ppif (top right table).
evidence: Analysis of publicly available RNAseq dataset on fracture shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In conditions leading to pathological calcification such as osteoarthritis and cardiac valve calcification, PPIF expression is decreased.
source: We also found that in conditions leading to pathological calcification such as osteoarthritis and osteophyte formation (Dunn et al., 2016) and cardiac valve calcification (Huang et al., 2019) and associated with upregulated BMP/Smad signaling, PPIF expression is decreased (bottom tables).
evidence: Analysis of publicly available datasets on pathological calcification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BMP2 levels are decreased in bones of aged mice compared to young mice.
source: Using immunofluorescence (IF), we indeed detected decreased levels of BMP2 in bones of aged mice when compared to young mice.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from bone samples of 3- and 18-month-old mice shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CypD levels are increased in bones of aged mice compared to young mice.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, levels of CypD correspondingly increased (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from bone samples of 3- and 18-month-old mice shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: BMP2 signal is significantly increased in the fracture callus at day 14 post-fracture compared to unfractured bone.
source: Consistent with the published RNAseq dataset described above (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, top right table), BMP2 signal was significantly increased in the callus at day 14 post-fracture when compared to the unfractured bone.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from fracture samples shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The increase in BMP2 signal in fracture callus at day 14 is accompanied by significant decrease in CypD signal.
source: The observed increase in BMP2 signal was accompanied by significant decrease in CypD signal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from fracture samples shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Previously published transcriptomic data and the authors' own studies indicate inverse correlation between BMP signaling and CypD expression.
source: Therefore, previously published transcriptomic data and our own studies indicate inverse correlation between BMP signaling and CypD expression.
evidence: Summary of multiple datasets and immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: CypD deletion produces protective effects against bone loss in aged mice.
source: Conversely, CypD deletion produces protective effects against several degenerative processes, including bone loss in aged mice (Shum et al., 2016a).
evidence: Reference to previous publication by the authors.

claim: Osteoblast-specific CypD deletion protects against bone loss in aging.
source: An important observation in this experimental design is that OB-specific CypD deletion is in fact protecting against bone loss in aging, corroborating our previous results when we investigated the effects of CypD global deletion in mice (Shum et al., 2016b).
evidence: Comparison of current conditional knockout data with previous global knockout data.

claim: Osteoblast-specific CypD deletion increases torsional rigidity in aged mice.
source: For instance, biomechanical testing showed increased torsional rigidity in control tibiae of Cre+ (Ppif-/-) mice when compared to Cre- (Ppif+/+) mice (Figure 7H), indicative of an increased bone strength.
evidence: Biomechanical torsion testing data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Osteoblast-specific CypD deletion increases bone volume fraction in aged mice.
source: Bone volume fraction measured with micro-computed tomography (μCT), a strong predictor of bone strength (Nazarian et al., 2008), provided further evidence that OB-specific CypD deletion effectively protects against bone degeneration in aging (Figure 7G).
evidence: Micro-CT data shown in Figure 7G with reference to bone strength prediction.

claim: AAV-DIO-delivered CypD re-expression decreases cortical thickness compared to contralateral PBS-injected tibiae.
source: Although bones with AAV-DIO-delivered CypD re-expression showed decreased cortical thickness and torsional rigidity when compared to their respective contralateral PBS-injected tibiae (Figure 7F and H)
evidence: Micro-CT and biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 7F and H.

claim: CypD re-expression in Cre+ mice significantly decreases normalized cortical thickness.
source: Normalized data showed a significant decrease in cortical thickness in the virus-infected Cre+ mice (Figure 7I)
evidence: Normalized micro-CT data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: CypD re-expression decreases tibial biomechanical properties and increases bone fragility in virus-injected bones from Cre+ mice compared to Cre- mice.
source: These changes were sufficient to decrease tibial biomechanical properties and increase bone fragility in virus-injected bones from Cre+ mice when compared to Cre- mice (Figure 7K–M).
evidence: Normalized biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 7K-M.

claim: CypD re-expression decreases osteocalcin immunofluorescence signal in vivo.
source: CypD re-expression and GOF also led to decreased OB function in vivo as confirmed by decreased osteocalcin IF (Figure 7D), recapitulating the results we have observed in vitro (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from bone sections shown in Figure 7D.

claim: CypD re-expression does not change osteoclast activity measured by TRAP staining.
source: Since OB function is described to partially regulate osteoclast formation, recruitment and maturation, we analyzed osteoclast activity by tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining (Figure 7E) and found no differences between the AAV-DIO-injected tibiae of Cre+ and Cre- mice.
evidence: TRAP staining data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Osteoblast-specific CypD re-expression and gain-of-function detrimentally affect osteoblast function and impair bone phenotype in aging.
source: Nonetheless, our aggregated data present strong evidence that OB-specific CypD re-expression and GOF detrimentally affect OB function and it is sufficient to impair bone phenotype in aging.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple in vivo measurements including micro-CT, biomechanics, and histology.

claim: The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) is a non-selective high-conductance channel within the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) is a non-selective high-conductance channel within the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about MPTP structure and location.

claim: MPTP opening leads to increased permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane and entry of solutes up to 1.5 kDa of molecular mass.
source: MPTP opening leads to the increased permeability of the IMM and entry of solutes up to 1.5 kDa of molecular mass, that is, mitochondrial permeability transition (Bernardi et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to published literature on MPTP function.

claim: CypD is the only genetically proven opener of the MPTP.
source: Currently, several MPTP opening effectors have been described, but the mitochondrial matrix protein cyclophilin D (CypD) remains the only genetically proven opener of the MPTP (Briston et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to published literature on CypD's role in MPTP.

claim: CypD is encoded by the nuclear gene PPIF.
source: Encoded by the nuclear gene PPIF, CypD is a chaperone protein – peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase F – thought to be involved in protein folding.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CypD gene and function.

claim: CypD is imported into mitochondria where it can actively bind to the mitochondrial ATP synthase, decreasing the threshold for pore opening and increasing opening probability.
source: Regarded as the master regulator of MPTP, CypD is imported into mitochondria where it can actively bind to the mitochondrial ATP synthase, decreasing the threshold for pore opening and increasing opening probability.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CypD mechanism of action.

claim: Post-translational modifications such as acetylation and phosphorylation exert regulatory properties on CypD activity and MPTP opening.
source: A range of post-translation modifications, such as acetylation and phosphorylation, is known to exert regulatory properties on CypD activity, and consequently on MPTP opening (Gutiérrez-Aguilar and Baines, 2015; Porter and Beutner, 2018; Amanakis and Murphy, 2020).
evidence: References to published literature on CypD post-translational regulation.

claim: CypD expression and activity are cell-specific.
source: CypD expression and activity are cell-specific (Laker et al., 2016) and can be regulated during differentiation.
evidence: Reference to published literature on cell-specific CypD expression.

claim: Higher ROS levels due to OxPhos activation can lead to MPTP opening and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Higher ROS levels due to OxPhos activation can lead to deleterious effects including opening of the MPTP and consequently blunting of mitochondrial function (Carraro and Bernardi, 2016).
evidence: Reference to published literature on ROS-induced MPTP opening.

claim: CypD downregulation has been reported during neuronal and cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: Such an inhibition due to downregulation of CypD has been reported during neuronal and cardiomyocyte differentiation (Eliseev et al., 2007; Hom et al., 2011; Lingan et al., 2017).
evidence: References to published literature on CypD downregulation during differentiation.

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming is accompanied by transient MPTP opening and CypD expression upregulation.
source: Conversely, induced pluripotent stem cell reprograming is accompanied by a metabolic shift from OxPhos to glycolysis and not surprisingly, by transient MPTP opening and CypD expression upregulation (Ying et al., 2018).
evidence: Reference to published literature on CypD during iPSC reprogramming.

claim: BMP signaling pathway is an important driver of cell differentiation and maturation.
source: The bone morphogenic protein (BMP) signaling pathway is an important driver of cell differentiation and maturation.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about BMP signaling.

claim: BMPs regulate processes from embryogenesis and development to adult tissue homeostasis.
source: BMPs are shown to regulate early processes from embryogenesis and development to adult tissue homeostasis.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about BMP function.

claim: Osteogenesis and osteoblast differentiation are controlled at least in part via BMP/Smad canonical signaling.
source: Osteogenesis and osteoblast (OB) differentiation are controlled at least in part via BMP/Smad canonical signaling.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about osteogenic differentiation.

claim: During osteogenic differentiation, activation of the transcription factor Runx2 is mediated by the BMP/Smad signaling pathway.
source: During osteogenic differentiation, activation of the transcription factor Runx2 is mediated by the BMP/Smad signaling pathway initiating a cascade of downstream osteogenic marker genes expression (Bianco and Robey, 2015).
evidence: Reference to published literature on Runx2 activation.

claim: Bone marrow stromal cells shift their bioenergetic profile toward OxPhos during osteoblast differentiation.
source: Our lab and others have demonstrated that bone marrow stromal (a.k.a. mesenchymal stem) cells (BMSCs) shift their bioenergetic profile toward OxPhos during OB differentiation (Shum et al., 2016a; Feigenson et al., 2017; Colaianni et al., 2018; Shares et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2019; Smith and Eliseev, 2021).
evidence: References to multiple published studies including authors' own work.

claim: Osteoblast function involves bone matrix deposition, an energy-consuming process highly dependent on mitochondrial bioenergetics and OxPhos activity.
source: Since OB function involves bone matrix deposition, an energy-consuming process highly dependent on mitochondrial bioenergetics and OxPhos activity, we hypothesized that MPTP inhibition via CypD transcriptional downregulation is mediated by BMP/Smad signaling and required to sustain OxPhos function and support osteogenic differentiation.
evidence: Established knowledge about osteoblast function combined with hypothesis.

claim: Differentiated osteoblasts produce more ROS due to higher OxPhos activity.
source: Since a higher OxPhos activity, as seen in differentiated OBs, is described to produce more ROS (Barja, 1999; Dröse and Brandt, 2012; Suski et al., 2018; Turrens, 1997; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: References to published literature and MitoSox data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Acetylation of CypD at K166 increases CypD activity and MPTP opening and can be mimicked by K166Q mutation.
source: It is known that acetylation of CypD at K166 increases CypD activity and MPTP opening and can be mimicked by K166Q mutation (Alkalaeva et al., 2009; Porter and Beutner, 2018).
evidence: References to published literature on CypD K166 acetylation.

claim: Smad7 competitively inhibits the interaction of R-Smads to the cytoplasmic domain of their respective cell receptors.
source: Smad7 competitively inhibits the interaction of R-Smads to the cytoplasmic domain of their respective cell receptors, therefore preventing R-Smad recruitment and phosphorylation, and consequently nuclear translocation.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about Smad7 mechanism of action.

claim: Smads can act as either promoter repressors or activators in a gene-specific manner.
source: This bi-directional effect of Smads on gene regulation is well described. Smads can either act as promoter repressors or activators in a gene-specific manner (Massagué et al., 2005).
evidence: Reference to published literature on Smad bidirectional regulation.

claim: Cell/tissue specification is driven by selective methylation of promoter regions which changes chromatin accessibility.
source: The tissue-specific effect of Smad1 on Ppif can be explained, for instance, by the fact that cell/tissue specification is driven by selective methylation of promoter regions which changes chromatin accessibility (Atlasi and Stunnenberg, 2017).
evidence: Reference to published literature on epigenetic regulation.

claim: BMP signaling is suppressed during myogenic differentiation showing marked upregulation of Noggin expression.
source: Interestingly, BMP signaling is suppressed during myogenic differentiation showing marked upregulation of Noggin expression (Ono et al., 2011).
evidence: Reference to published literature on BMP signaling in myogenesis.

claim: CypD deletion is shown to present a protective phenotype against aging in several tissue-specific mouse models.
source: CypD deletion is shown to present a protective phenotype against aging in several tissue-specific mouse models.
evidence: General statement based on multiple published studies.

claim: CypD ablation in mice resulted in diminished disease progression for reperfusion injury of the heart and brain, axonopathy, and other neurodegenerative and demyelinating diseases.
source: Additionally, CypD ablation in mice also resulted in diminished disease progression for some pathologies, such as reperfusion injury of the heart and brain, axonopathy, and other neurodegenerative and demyelinating diseases (Baines et al., 2005; Schinzel et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2010; Halestrap and Richardson, 2015; Ahier et al., 2018; Gauba et al., 2019).
evidence: References to multiple published studies on CypD deletion effects.

claim: Cardiomyocytes unable to downregulate CypD during embryonic development can cause congenital heart defects.
source: Cardiomyocytes unable of downregulating CypD during embryonic development can cause congenital heart defects, secondary to defects in MPTP activity and myocyte differentiation (Hom et al., 2011; Lingan et al., 2017).
evidence: References to published studies on CypD in cardiac development.

claim: The progression of Alzheimer's disease is accelerated by higher CypD levels and MPTP activity.
source: The progression of Alzheimer's disease is accelerated by higher CypD levels and MPTP activity, leading to further mitochondrial stress and neuronal exhaustion (Alavian et al., 2014; Gauba et al., 2019).
evidence: References to published studies on CypD in Alzheimer's disease.

claim: Treatment with CypD inhibitors can reverse collagen VI myopathies.
source: Collagen VI myopathies are well described and established pathologies where CypD overexpression plays a major role, and as expected, treatment with CypD inhibitors can reverse the disease (Giorgio et al., 2010; Zulian et al., 2014).
evidence: References to published studies on CypD inhibitors in myopathies.

claim: Higher OxPhos in BMSCs correlates with better spinal fusion outcomes in both human patients and in a mouse model.
source: Not surprisingly, we recently reported that higher OxPhos in BMSCs correlates with better spinal fusion outcomes in both human patients and in a mouse model (Laura et al., 2020).
evidence: Reference to authors' previous publication.

claim: OxPhos is activated while MPTP is inhibited via CypD downregulation during osteoblast differentiation.
source: Taken together, the evidence collected in other groups' studies, our previous studies, and the present study points that OxPhos is activated while MPTP is inhibited via CypD downregulation during OB differentiation.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating current and previous studies.

claim: Bones from aged mice present higher CypD levels when compared to young mice.
source: Additionally, we found that bones from aged mice present higher CypD levels when compared to young mice.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from aged vs young mouse bones.

claim: CypD/MPTP upregulation is present in several tissues during aging and plays a role in the onset and progression of several degenerative pathologies.
source: This result goes along with studies showing that CypD/MPTP upregulation is present in several tissues during aging and as discussed, such upregulation plays a role in the onset and progression of several degenerative pathologies.
evidence: General statement based on literature review and current findings.

claim: CypD overexpression for a period of 2 months was sufficient to decrease bone mechanical properties in aged mice.
source: Even though aged skeleton is characterized by a very low turnover rate, CypD overexpression for a total period of only 2 months was sufficient to decrease bone mechanical properties.
evidence: Biomechanical testing data from in vivo CypD re-expression experiment.

claim: The BMP/Smad-Ppif axis is relevant for pathological ossification/calcification conditions such as osteoarthritis and cardiac valve calcification.
source: Additionally, RNAseq data from pathological ossification/calcification conditions, such as osteoarthritis and osteophyte formation (Dunn et al., 2016) and cardiac valve calcification (Huang et al., 2019), suggested the inverse correlation between BMP signaling and CypD expression in these pathologies. Therefore, the BMP/Smad-Ppif axis is also relevant for these pathological conditions and can be aimed as a potential therapeutic target as well.
evidence: Analysis of published RNAseq datasets on pathological calcification.

claim: CypD inhibitors can protect against injury after reperfusion in heart and brain in animal models.
source: Studies in the heart and brain have shown that CypD inhibitors can protect against injury after reperfusion in animal models (Halestrap and Richardson, 2015; Warne et al., 2016).
evidence: References to published studies on CypD inhibitors.

claim: Lack of target validation and understanding of CypD regulatory pathway has contributed to failed Phase III clinical trials.
source: However, the lack of target validation and better understanding of CypD regulatory pathway has contributed to failed Phase III clinical trials (Nighoghossian et al., 2015; Ong et al., 2017; Briston et al., 2019).
evidence: References to published clinical trial reports.
